cards.front: 1000 amide sites. In each time slice, 30% of the sites that are STILL unexchanged exchange. After 2 slices: how many are unexchanged, what fraction is exchanged, and what does the factor 0.7 stand for?
cards.back: Method: each slice multiplies the unexchanged count by the survival factor (1 − p) = 0.7, i.e. the fraction of still-unexchanged sites that stay unexchanged through one slice. After 2 slices: 1000 × 0.7^2 = 490 unexchanged. Exchanged = 1 − 0.49 = 0.51 (510 sites). A product of (1 − p) factors is always the SURVIVING fraction; exchanged is 1 minus it.

cards.front: A site exchanges with rate $k$. In a tiny slice of width $dt$, what is $k\,dt$ the probability of, and for which sites does it apply?
cards.back: $k\,dt$ is the probability that a site which is still unexchanged at the start of the slice exchanges during that slice. It applies only to the current survivors, not the original population. Reason: $k$ = (number leaving)/(number present × time), so $k\,dt$ = fraction of the present pool that leaves.

cards.front: Tube of $N_0$ unexchanged sites, rate $k$, slice width $dt$. Compute the number exchanging in slice 1, slice 2 and slice 3, and the survivors after each. (Example: $N_0 = 500$, $k = 4$ per s, $dt = 0.05$ s.)
cards.back: Method: $k\,dt$ = per-slice fraction of the CURRENT pool that exchanges. Each slice: exchanged $= k\,dt \times U_{\text{start}}$, survivors $= U_{\text{start}} - \text{exchanged} = U_{\text{start}}(1-k\,dt)$. Example: $k\,dt = 0.2$; slice 1: $100$ exchange, $400$ left; slice 2: $80$, $320$ left; slice 3: $64$, $256$ left. Survivors after $n$ slices $= N_0 (1-k\,dt)^n$.

history.note: The exchange counts per slice are never given; only survivors are shown. Slice 3 is also truncated to $409$ rather than $409.6$.
No attempt: neither the exchanged-in-slice column nor the survivors-after-slice column was filled for any slice.
Override again→hard: learner declined the retry to end the session; not a knowledge miss. Earlier this session the method was correct, only the exchanged column was omitted.

cards.front: Why is the fraction still unexchanged after two slices $(1-k\,dt)^2$ and not $1 - 2k\,dt$ or $(k\,dt)^2$?
cards.back: Each slice, a fraction $1-k\,dt$ of the sites present at its start survive. Surviving both slices means surviving slice 1 and then slice 2, applied to the pool slice 1 left behind: $(1-k\,dt)(1-k\,dt)$. $(k\,dt)^2$ would be 'exchanged twice', impossible; $1-2k\,dt$ ignores that the second slice acts on a smaller pool.

history.note: No reason is given for why $(1-k\,dt)^2$ is exact.
Override: grader penalised missing justification for A, which the prompt did not ask for. A, B, C all correctly identified; learner then supplied the sequential-survival reason for A in chat.
No reason is given for why $(1-k\,dt)^2$ is correct (survival of slice 1, then of slice 2 applied to what slice 1 left).

Override: the prompt did not ask to justify A; A, B ("incorrect expansion of a" = first-order truncation), C all correctly identified. Same pattern as last session; card front should not demand justification of A separately.

cards.front: From the one-slice rule $U_{\text{new}} = U - k\,dt\,U$, derive $\frac{dU}{dt} = -kU$ and say why the ratio $(U_{\text{new}}-U)/dt$ does not vanish as $dt \to 0$.
cards.back: Subtract $U$: $U_{\text{new}} - U = -k\,dt\,U$ (keep the minus: survivors fall). Divide by $dt$: $(U_{\text{new}}-U)/dt = -kU$, exactly, for every $dt$, because the numerator contains $dt$ as a factor and it cancels. As $dt \to 0$ the left side is by definition $dU/dt$. Meaning: survivors vanish at a speed proportional to their number. Example: $U=1000$, $k=2$: ratio is $-2000$/s whether $dt = 0.05$ or $0.000001$.

history.note: The jump from $U_n - U = -k\,dt\,U$ straight to $\frac{dU}{dt} = -kU$ omits dividing by $dt$ (giving $\frac{U_n - U}{dt} = -kU$) and taking $dt \to 0$.
Override hard→good: paper skipped the explicit divide-by-dt line and wrote "change the same amount"; in chat he gave the correct reason (RHS −kU independent of dt). Watch the "same amount" phrasing.

cards.front: Why is the survivor fraction after time $t$ equal to $e^{-kt}$ rather than $1 - kt$? Where does the $e$ come from?
cards.back: Exact slice answer: $(1-k\,dt)^n$ with $n = t/dt$ slices, i.e. $(1 - kt/n)^n$, which tends to $e^{-kt}$ as $n \to \infty$ (e.g. $0.999^{1000} \approx 0.368 = e^{-1}$). $1 - kt$ is the single-fat-slice answer: it bills $k\,dt$ against the starting pool for the whole stretch while the pool actually drains inside the slice, so it over-removes and goes negative past $t = 1/k$. Only infinitely thin slices, rebilling against the current pool, get it right; that limit is $e^{-kt}$. Check: $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-kt} = -k e^{-kt}$ satisfies $dU/dt = -kU$.

history.note: The answer never explains why $1-kt$ fails or where $e$ comes from. It solves $\frac{dU}{dt}=-kU$ to get $e^{-kt}$ without connecting this to compounding $(1-kt/n)^n$ or its $n\to\infty$ limit.
In (a), 'many small slices' is given without saying each slice removes $k\,dt$ of the current survivors rather than of the original pool.

cards.front: For first-order exchange with rate $k$, what are the three quantities $1 - e^{-kt}$, $k e^{-kt}$ and $1/k$, and which of them can exceed 1?
cards.back: $1 - e^{-kt}$: fraction exchanged by time $t$ (cumulative probability, dimensionless, $\le 1$). $k e^{-kt}$: density, probability PER SECOND of exchanging around time $t$; units 1/s, so it can exceed 1 (e.g. $k = 5$/s gives $f(0) = 5$/s). $1/k$: mean lifetime, $\int_0^\infty t\,k e^{-kt}dt$. Only the density can exceed 1, because it is a rate, not a probability; $f(t)\,dt$ is the probability of exchanging in the thin slice at $t$.

history.note: Calling $1/k$ the half-life. The question of which expressions can exceed 1 was also never answered.
No units are given for any of the three expressions. The first substantive error is claiming $1/k$ can exceed 1, when the rubric expects only $ke^{-kt}$. Here $1/k = 0.25\,\mathrm{s}$.

Override again→hard: all three named correctly, mean lifetime (not half-life) fixed since last time; 1/k > 1 is actually fine (it is a time). Gap: density > 1 justified by 'integrates to 1' instead of units 1/s and f(t)dt being the probability.

cards.front: A site has $k = 0.1$ per second. Someone says 'so it has a 10% chance of exchanging in the first second.' Compute the actual probability and explain the gap. (Use $e^{-0.1} \approx 0.905$.)
cards.back: Actual: $1 - e^{-kt} = 1 - 0.905 = 0.095$, slightly less than $kt = 0.1$. $kt$ is the one-fat-slice answer: it charges $k\,dt$ against the starting pool for the whole second, but the pool drains during the second, so it over-removes. Exact answer comes from infinitely thin slices rebilled against the current pool, which is $e^{-kt}$. The gap grows with $kt$: at $kt = 1$, $0.63$ vs $1$.

history.note: $1-0.607$ was evaluated as $0.303$ instead of $0.393$.

cards.front: Transition matrix $P$ with rows = from-state, columns = to-state. Given a count vector $v$ over the states, compute the counts after one step and say what each term in the sum counts. (Example: states $C, O$; $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.8 & 0.2\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}$, $v = (800, 200)$.)
cards.back: $v_{\text{new}} = v P$, row vector on the left: $(vP)_j = \sum_i v_i P_{ij}$. Each term $v_i P_{ij}$ = sites that were in $i$ times the fraction that moved to $j$; column $j$ collects all inflows into $j$. Example: $C$: $800\cdot0.8 + 200\cdot0.5 = 640 + 100 = 740$ (closed that stayed + open that closed); $O$: $800\cdot0.2 + 200\cdot0.5 = 260$. Rows sum to 1, so the total (1000) is conserved. Writing the vector as a column and multiplying $P v$ gives the wrong answer (680, 500).

history.note: Part 3: the answer describes the totals $330$ and $70$ rather than the two terms $270$ and $60$ that make up the new $F$ count.

In (b), the two terms are left as symbols $\phi_{A\to A}$ and $\phi_{B\to A}$ without being identified as $540$ and $160$. Separately, the boxed B count in (a) is illegible and could read $700$ instead of $300$.

Override hard→good: page 1 showed 0.9·600 + 0.4·400 explicitly, so the terms were numerically present; grader penalised the split between (a) and (b) and an unclear digit. Learner frustrated by the follow-up.

cards.front: Three-state chain $C$ (closed), $O$ (open), $X$ (exchanged, absorbing), rows = FROM. Given $P$ and a count vector $v$, compute $vP$ and explain why the total is conserved but can still hide an error. (Example: $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1&0\\0.6&0.3&0.1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $v=(500,300,200)$.)
cards.back: Row vector on the left: entry $j$ of $vP$ sums $v_i P_{ij}$ over all FROM-states $i$, i.e. every inflow into $j$. Example: $C' = 450+180 = 630$, $O' = 50+90 = 140$, $X' = 0 + 30 + 200 = 230$ (the 30 = open sites that exchanged; $X$ row $(0,0,1)$ means nothing leaves $X$). Total 1000 is conserved because each row of $P$ sums to 1, so the total check only catches errors that don't offset: re-read each column entry against the matrix.

history.note: Part (b): the justification appeals to the transpose having 'the same conservation property' rather than to row sums of $P$ equalling 1 and to offsetting errors in entries.

cards.front: Two-state chain $C \rightleftharpoons O$ with per-step probabilities $p$ ($C \to O$) and $q$ ($O \to C$). Find the stationary split $\pi$ and say what 'stationary' means for individual sites. (Example: $p = 0.2$, $q = 0.5$.)
cards.back: Stationary = the step rule maps the distribution to itself, $\pi P = \pi$, i.e. flows balance: sites leaving $C$ equal sites returning, $p\,\pi_C = q\,\pi_O$, so $\pi_C/\pi_O = q/p$. Example: $\pi_C/\pi_O = 2.5$, $\pi = (5/7, 2/7) \approx (0.714, 0.286)$. Individual sites keep flipping; only the counts are fixed. $\pi_O/\pi_C = K_{op}$ in HDX.

history.note: Second row of $P$ is written as $(0.7, 0.3)$, but an open site closes with probability $0.3$, so the row should be $(0.3, 0.7)$. Then $\pi$ is computed by averaging columns, $\pi_C = \frac{0.9+0.7}{2}$, which is not a stationarity condition.
Used flow balance k_op C = k_cl O unprompted in the EX2 derivation (rate form), correct.

cards.front: How does the rate matrix $Q$ arise from the step matrix $P$, and why do the rows of $Q$ sum to zero?
cards.back: Over a tiny slice, each jump $i \to j$ has probability $k_{ij}\,dt$ (the rate definition), so $P(dt) = I + Q\,dt$ with off-diagonal $Q_{ij} = k_{ij}$ and diagonal $Q_{ii} = -\sum_{j \ne i} k_{ij}$ (minus total exit rate). Rows of $P$ sum to 1, so rows of $Q\,dt = P - I$ sum to 0. $Q$ is independent of $dt$; it is the chain itself. Master equation: $dv/dt = vQ$, the matrix version of $dU/dt = -kU$.

history.note: $Q_{ii}$ is described as the rate of jumping back into state $i$ ($i \to i$).
The boxed formula $P(dt) = Q\,dt$ omits the identity: it should be $P(dt) = I + Q\,dt$.

cards.front: Write the rate matrix $Q$ for the HDX chain $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ (rates $k_{op}$, $k_{cl}$, $k_{ch}$; $X$ absorbing) and read off $dX/dt$ from $dv/dt = vQ$.
cards.back: Rows = FROM, order $C,O,X$: $Q = \begin{pmatrix} -k_{op} & k_{op} & 0 \\ k_{cl} & -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) & k_{ch} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The $O$ diagonal is minus the total exit rate (two exits). The $X$ row is zero because nothing leaves $X$. The $X$ column of $vQ$ gives $dX/dt = k_{ch}\,O(t)$: exchange only happens from the open state. $vQ$ is a row vector of three derivatives, not a sum.

history.note: Part (a), third row: $Q_{XX} = 1$; the absorbing state's row must be $(0, 0, 0)$.

cards.front: Chain $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ with $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ per second (closing much faster than exchange). Derive $k_{obs}$ from $dX/dt = k_{ch} O$, stating what fixes $O$ and why.
cards.back: Method: an open site exchanges with share $k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 10/110 \approx 0.09$ per opening, so it hops $C \rightleftharpoons O$ about eleven times per leak; the pair settles to flow balance $k_{op}C = k_{cl}O$, i.e. $O = K_{op} C \approx K_{op} U$ with $K_{op} = k_{op}/k_{cl} = 0.01$. Then $dX/dt = k_{ch} K_{op} U$, so $k_{obs} = K_{op} k_{ch} = 0.1$ per s. This is EX2.

history.note: In (b), the boxed line $\frac{dX}{dt} = \frac{U}{25} = k_{obs}$ equates $k_{obs}$ with $U/25$ instead of identifying $k_{obs} = 1/25 = 0.04\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Earlier, in (a), the balance is used as $O/C = k_{op}/k_{cl}$ but never named as the flow balance $k_{op}C = k_{cl}O$.

cards.front: In $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$, two inequalities often hold: $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ and $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$. Which one is the EX2 condition, and what does the other one do?
cards.back: $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$ is the EX2 condition: the exchange share per opening $k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$ is small, so the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ hop repeats many times before a leak and the pair settles to its balance. $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ only makes $O$ small ($C \approx U$); it says nothing about settling. Same $k_{op}, k_{cl}$ with $k_{ch}$ raised from 10 to $10^4$ flips EX2 to EX1 while $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ stays true.

cards.front: EX1 limit of $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$: what is $k_{obs}$, which inequality does it need, and what happens to $k_{obs}$ if instead $k_{cl} = k_{ch}$?
cards.back: $k_{obs} = k_{op}$, needing $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$: an open site exchanges before it can close, so every opening is a one-way trip $C \to O \to X$ and $X$ grows at the opening rate. In general $k_{obs} \approx k_{op} \cdot k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$, the opening rate times the exchange share per opening; with $k_{cl} = k_{ch}$ that share is $1/2$, so $k_{obs} \approx k_{op}/2$.

cards.front: Chain $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ with $k_{op} = 2$, $k_{cl} = 30$, $k_{ch} = 70$ per second. (1) Write $dO/dt$ as inflow minus outflow with numbers. (2) Give the steady-state $O$ as a multiple of $C$. (3) State the one rate comparison that justifies $dO/dt \approx 0$.
cards.back: Method: inflow to $O$ is openings, $k_{op}C$; outflow is every exit from $O$, $(k_{cl}+k_{ch})O$. So $dO/dt = 2C - 100\,O$. Set to zero: $O = \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}C = 0.02\,C$. Justified because the total exit rate from $O$ ($100$/s, lifetime 0.01 s) is much larger than the inflow rate constant $k_{op} = 2$/s, so $O$ settles far faster than $C$ changes. Which exit is bigger ($k_{cl}$ or $k_{ch}$) does not matter; only their sum versus $k_{op}$. Watch the arrow directions: $k_{op}$ feeds $O$, $k_{cl}$ and $k_{ch}$ drain it.

history.note: $\frac{dO}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dt}Q\big|_O = 5\frac{dC}{dt} - 250\frac{dO}{dt}$: the product should be $VQ$ (populations), not $\frac{dV}{dt}Q$, which should give $5C - 250\,O$.
Part (3): the comparison is stated as $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ instead of $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}+k_{ch}$, and the reason why it matters is not given.

cards.front: For $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$, write $k_{obs}$ as (opening rate) × (fraction of openings that exchange). What is that fraction, and why is it not $k_{ch}/k_{cl}$?
cards.back: $k_{obs} \approx k_{op}\cdot\dfrac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$. The fraction is the exchange exit over the *total* exits from $O$ (closing plus exchange). $k_{ch}/k_{cl}$ is only the EX2 approximation to it, valid when $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$; in general it can exceed 1, which is impossible for a fraction, and would give $k_{obs} > k_{op}$, impossible since a site cannot exchange faster than it opens. Limits: $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$ gives $K_{op}k_{ch}$ (EX2); $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$ gives $k_{op}$ (EX1). Full form with the $O$ correction: $k_{op}k_{ch}/(k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch})$.

history.note: The explanation never identifies $k_{cl}+k_{ch}$ as the total exit rate from O. It also never says why $k_{ch}/k_{cl}$ fails in general: it holds only when $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$ and can otherwise exceed 1.

cards.front: $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ with $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 200$, $k_{ch} = 50$ per second. Compute $k_{obs}$ from the general formula, then say which limit (EX1 or EX2) it is closer to and what each limiting formula would have given.
cards.back: Method: share of openings that exchange $= k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 50/250 = 0.2$, so $k_{obs} = k_{op}\times 0.2 = 0.2$/s (three-term: $50/251 \approx 0.199$/s). Closer to EX2 since $k_{ch} < k_{cl}$: EX2 formula $K_{op}k_{ch} = (1/200)(50) = 0.25$/s (20% high because $k_{ch}$ is not ≪ $k_{cl}$); EX1 formula $k_{op} = 1$/s (far off). The general formula interpolates between them.

cards.front: Raising pH moves an amide from EX2 toward EX1. Which of $k_{op}, k_{cl}, k_{ch}$ does pH change, by how much per unit, and why does that change the regime in that direction?
cards.back: Only $k_{ch}$: above pH ~3 exchange is base-catalysed, $k_{ch} \propto [\mathrm{OH^-}]$, so ten-fold per pH unit. $k_{op}$ and $k_{cl}$ are protein motions and stay fixed. The regime is the race between the two exits from $O$: share of openings that exchange $= k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. Raising $k_{ch}/k_{cl}$ makes exchange win before closing, the share $\to 1$, $k_{obs} \to k_{op}$ (EX1). Experimental signature: in EX2 $k_{obs}$ scales ten-fold per pH unit; in EX1 it stops responding to pH. The crossover pH is where $k_{ch} = k_{cl}$.

cards.front: A segment of $N$ amides opens as a unit. Why does EX2 give a single isotope hump that slides gradually, while EX1 gives two fixed peaks that trade heights? Name the statistical ingredient and the quantity both envelopes share.
cards.back: Per opening, each exposed site exchanges with probability $s = k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. EX2 ($s \ll 1$): at most one site per opening, so sites accumulate exchange independently over many openings; deuteron count is $\mathrm{Bin}(N, 1-e^{-k_{obs}t})$, one hump sliding from 0 to $N$. EX1 ($s \approx 1$): every opening exchanges all $N$ sites, so molecules are all-or-nothing: spikes at $+0$ and $+N$, heights $e^{-k_{op}t}$ and $1-e^{-k_{op}t}$. Ingredient: independent vs perfectly correlated coin flips. Both share the centroid $N(1-e^{-k_{obs}t})$, so centroid alone cannot distinguish them; width/shape can. Extra slowly-interconverting populations each add their own mode.

cards.front: Rate matrix $Q = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$ per second (rows = from). Find a left eigenvector $v$ with $vQ = 0$ and state what it represents physically and why.
cards.back: Method: write $(a,b)Q = (-2a+3b,\ 2a-3b)$ and set to zero: $a = \tfrac{3}{2}b$, so $v \propto (3,2)$, i.e. 60%/40%. Meaning: $vQ = 0$ is the same as $\dot p = 0$ for $p \propto v$, so this is the stationary distribution: the one split where every flux balances ($2\cdot 3 = 3\cdot 2$) and nothing changes in time ($e^{0\cdot t} = 1$). Use left eigenvectors because $p$ is a row multiplying $Q$ from the left; eigenvalues of $Q$ carry units of per second.

cards.front: For $\dot p = pQ$, suppose $p(0) = c_0\, v$ where $v$ is a left eigenvector, $vQ = \lambda v$, $v \neq 0$. What is $p(t)$, and what two facts does the derivation use?
cards.back: $p(t) = c_0 e^{\lambda t} v$: direction fixed, only the coefficient changes. Substitute $p = c v$: left side $\dot c\, v$, right side $(cv)Q = c(vQ) = \lambda c\, v$. Cancel the nonzero $v$: $\dot c = \lambda c$, so $c = c_0 e^{\lambda t}$. Uses (1) eigenvector property $vQ = \lambda v$, (2) scalar ODE solution.

cards.front: $Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ has left eigenvectors $(0.8, 0.2)$ with $\lambda = 0$ and $(1,-1)$ with $\lambda = -5$. Starting from $p(0) = (0.9, 0.1)$, write $p(t)$ exactly.
cards.back: Method: split $p(0)$ into eigenvectors, then multiply each piece by $e^{\lambda t}$. $(0.9, 0.1) = (0.8, 0.2) + 0.1\,(1,-1)$, so $p(t) = (0.8, 0.2) + 0.1\, e^{-5t}\,(1,-1)$. The stationary piece never changes; the zero-sum deviation decays at $5$/s. In two states every deviation between normalized populations is a multiple of $(1,-1)$, so relaxation is a single exponential.

cards.front: Why is the eigenvector $(1,-1)$ of a 2-state rate matrix not a population, and why do we still care about it?
cards.back: It has a negative entry and sums to zero, so it is a deviation (extra in A, same amount missing from B), not a distribution. Every real start is the stationary split plus a multiple of it, and that multiple decays as $e^{\lambda t}$ with its own eigenvalue, so it is the relaxation mode. Scalar multiples (e.g. $(-2,2)$) are the same eigenvector with the same eigenvalue.

cards.front: Superposition for $\dot p = pQ$: given left eigenvectors $v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$ that span the space, state the two-step recipe for $p(t)$ from an arbitrary $p(0)$, and name the two facts that make it valid.
cards.back: (1) Expand $p(0) = \sum_i c_i v_i$ (solve the linear system for the $c_i$). (2) $p(t) = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$. Valid because (a) linearity: $(\sum c_i v_i)Q = \sum c_i (v_i Q)$, so modes evolve separately; (b) each mode obeys $\dot c_i = \lambda_i c_i$ (eigenvector property), solved by $c_i e^{\lambda_i t}$.

cards.front: Substitute $p = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2$ into $\dot p = pQ$, where $v_1 Q = \lambda_1 v_1$ and $v_2 Q = \lambda_2 v_2$ are independent. Derive the ODE for $c_2(t)$ and say which fact justifies each step.
cards.back: Right side: $pQ = c_1(v_1Q) + c_2(v_2Q) = \lambda_1 c_1 v_1 + \lambda_2 c_2 v_2$ (linearity, then eigenvector property). Left side: $\dot p = \dot c_1 v_1 + \dot c_2 v_2$ (the $v_i$ are constant). Equate and match coefficients, allowed because $v_1, v_2$ are linearly independent so the expansion is unique: $\dot c_2 = \lambda_2 c_2$, hence $c_2(t) = c_2(0) e^{\lambda_2 t}$. Example: $Q = ((-2,2),(1,-1))$, $v_2 = (1,-1)$, $\lambda_2 = -3$ gives $\dot c_2 = -3 c_2$.

cards.front: A $3\times 3$ rate matrix has only two independent left eigenvectors $v_1, v_2$. Which step of the superposition recipe fails for a $p(0)$ outside their plane, and in what sense does it fail? When is this failure guaranteed not to happen?
cards.back: The expansion step: no $c_1, c_2$ exist with $p(0) = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2$ (the component system is inconsistent, e.g. $0 = 0.2$), not merely hard to solve. The pure sum of exponentials then does not describe the solution (a $t e^{\lambda t}$ term appears). It cannot happen when the $n$ eigenvalues are distinct: eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent and span.

cards.front: Why does $v\,e^{Qt} = e^{\lambda t} v$ for a left eigenvector $v$ with $vQ = \lambda v$? Give the one-line reason using the series $e^{Qt} = \sum_k (Qt)^k/k!$.
cards.back: Applying $vQ = \lambda v$ repeatedly gives $vQ^k = \lambda^k v$, so every term of the series becomes $\frac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!} v$; the fixed vector factors out and the scalar series $\sum (\lambda t)^k/k! = e^{\lambda t}$ remains. This is why $p(0)e^{Qt}$ with $p(0) = \sum c_i v_i$ equals the superposition $\sum c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$: $e^{Qt}$ is the superposition recipe written as one matrix.

cards.front: $V$ has the left eigenvectors of $Q$ as rows, $\Lambda$ the eigenvalues on the diagonal, so $VQ = \Lambda V$. A colleague concludes $Q = V\Lambda V^{-1}$ and $e^{Qt} = V e^{\Lambda t} V^{-1}$. Right or wrong, and why?
cards.back: Wrong order. To isolate $Q$ from $VQ = \Lambda V$ you must multiply on the LEFT by $V^{-1}$, because $V$ sits to the left of $Q$ and only $V^{-1}V = I$ cancels it there. So $Q = V^{-1}\Lambda V$, $Q^k = V^{-1}\Lambda^k V$, $e^{Qt} = V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} V$. The $t=0$ check (both give $I$) cannot catch the error; a row-sum or $t\to\infty$ check on a generic example does. ($V\Lambda V^{-1}$ is the form for eigenvectors as COLUMNS.)

cards.front: $Q = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ with left eigenvectors $v_1 = (1,2)$, $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $v_2 = (1,-1)$, $\lambda_2 = -3$. Compute $e^{Qt}$ explicitly via $V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} V$ and run two sanity checks.
cards.back: Method: $V = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $\det V = -3$, $V^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. $V^{-1}e^{\Lambda t}$ scales COLUMN $j$ of $V^{-1}$ by $e^{\lambda_j t}$ (equivalently $e^{\Lambda t}V$ scales ROW $j$ of $V$). Result: $e^{Qt} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac13 + \frac23 e^{-3t} & \frac23 - \frac23 e^{-3t} \\ \frac13 - \frac13 e^{-3t} & \frac23 + \frac13 e^{-3t} \end{pmatrix}$. Checks: $t=0$ gives $I$; every row sums to 1 (the $\lambda=0$ mode conserves probability); $t\to\infty$ rows $\to (1/3, 2/3) \propto v_1$ (stationary split); $\frac{d}{dt}$ at $0$ equals $Q$ ($e^{Qt} \approx I + Qt$). A row not summing to 1 means a slip.
